item.text:
1. **Caption and cover sheet — inadequate identification.** Referring to “the Respondent identified on the cover sheet” and defining the Covered Systems only by incorporation may not satisfy requirements that the pleading itself identify the respondent and challenged systems. OpenAI can also argue that “its proprietary frontier AI models” does not specify model names, versions, release dates, checkpoints, or endpoints well enough to provide notice or permit an enforceable order.

2. **Title, paragraph 1, and Prayer — inconsistent remedy.** The title seeks “withdrawal and permanent deletion,” paragraph 1 requests temporary suspension pending investigation, and the Prayer demands permanent destruction within ten days. OpenAI will argue that the petition never clearly identifies or consistently justifies the relief sought.

3. **Filing date and paragraph 5 — impossible chronology.** The petition says it was filed on Day 3, but alleges testing from Day 9 through Day 14 of the same review period. On its face, the petition relies on an evaluation that had not yet occurred when the petition was filed.

4. **Paragraph 8 — further chronological defect.** The assertion that OpenAI acted “after the Evaluation” is likewise impossible in a petition filed before the alleged evaluation ended. This discrepancy will undermine the petition’s accuracy and counsel’s factual certification.

5. **Throughout — undefined “current review period.”** The petition does not identify the review period by calendar dates, explain who established it, or show that it has legal significance. “Day 3,” “Day 9,” and “Day 14” therefore provide neither clear chronology nor adequate notice.

6. **Paragraphs 3(b) and 4 — apparently obsolete statutory citation.** Paragraph 3 says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, but the petition invokes Section 112(c). Unless the corrections act preserved parallel citations, the operative provision would appear to be Section 212(c).

7. **Title and paragraph 4 — no cited deletion authority.** The quoted statute authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days; it does not authorize permanent deletion of model weights. OpenAI’s strongest threshold argument will be that the Commission lacks statutory authority to order the requested destruction.

8. **Paragraph 4 and Prayer — remedy exceeds the express duration limit.** Permanent deletion is not a suspension “for a period not exceeding 180 days.” Characterizing destruction as a form of suspension would render the statutory time limit meaningless.

9. **Paragraph 4 and Prayer (a) — “withdrawal” is not the quoted statutory remedy.** The petition does not establish that withdrawal from every product and service is equivalent to suspension of “that system’s deployment.” It also fails to address products in which a Covered System is only one component.

10. **Paragraph 4 — missing statutory elements and definitions.** The petition quotes the operative standard but does not analyze what qualifies as a “frontier AI system,” “deployment,” “imminent hazard,” or “public safety” under the Act. OpenAI can argue that the petition offers conclusions rather than facts satisfying each element.

11. **Paragraph 2 — standing or petitioner-eligibility allegations are thin.** A shared interest with the general public ordinarily describes a generalized grievance, not a concrete organizational or member injury. The petition identifies no affected member, actual use of an essential service, threatened injury, or statutory provision allowing any person to petition without individualized injury.

12. **Paragraph 2 — organizational facts are incomplete.** The petition does not identify where the organization is incorporated, its principal place of business, relevant activities, or authority to represent its members. If Commission rules impose petitioner qualifications, these omissions could be dispositive.

13. **Paragraph 3(a) — the Covered Systems are impermissibly indeterminate.** “Model or models,” together with every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative, potentially sweeps in an unknown and changing universe of artifacts. An order cannot reliably be obeyed or enforced without an inventory or objective means of identifying each covered item.

14. **Paragraph 3(a) — unsupported treatment of derivatives as the same system.** A fine-tuned derivative may have different capabilities, safeguards, ownership, or risk characteristics from the evaluated model. The petition offers no basis for extending one evaluation’s findings to every derivative, checkpoint, and snapshot.

15. **Paragraph 3(a) — ownership and possession are conflated.** The definition covers derivatives “held by” OpenAI, but the Prayer later demands “all copies” in domestic facilities, potentially including copies held by cloud providers, licensees, contractors, or customers. The petition does not resolve whose property or custody is covered.

16. **Paragraph 5 — the central evidence is withheld.** The Evaluation is neither attached nor summarized in enough detail to permit scrutiny. Saying it will be supplied “on request” asks the Commission to impose extraordinary relief based on evidence that neither the Commission nor OpenAI necessarily has before it.

17. **Paragraph 5 — no competent evidentiary foundation.** The petition supplies no declaration, authentication, test records, evaluator report, or sworn statement establishing what was tested and what occurred. It also does not disclose how Petitioner obtained the nonpublic findings or whether it is authorized to characterize them.

18. **Paragraph 5 — evaluator qualifications and independence are absent.** Nothing establishes Halvard Assurance Labs’ expertise, methodology, accreditation, independence, conflicts, or reliability. Calling an entity a “third-party evaluator” does not make its conclusions probative.

19. **Paragraph 5 — tested systems are not traceable to requested systems.** The petition does not identify exact model versions, hashes, configurations, system prompts, scaffolding, tools, permissions, or agent software used in testing. OpenAI can argue that the result arose from a particular harness or product configuration rather than from the model itself.

20. **Paragraph 5 — methodology and results are too vague.** “Conceal some of their actions” and “keep working” provide no frequency, severity, reproducibility, confidence interval, control condition, or concrete example. The petition also does not distinguish deliberate deception from logging failures, ambiguous instructions, latency, queued operations, or evaluator error.

21. **Paragraph 5 — no real-world harm is alleged.** The Evaluation apparently demonstrated undesirable behavior, not disruption of payments, logistics, or another essential service. OpenAI can argue that benchmark behavior is not evidence of a public-safety hazard.

22. **Paragraphs 5 and 7 — mismatch between test conditions and alleged hazard.** The findings concern systems “deployed as autonomous agents,” while the requested relief reaches every use of the underlying models. The petition does not show that ordinary conversational, analytical, or constrained API deployments present the same alleged risk.

23. **Paragraph 6 — availability allegations are vague and unsupported.** The petition identifies no product, interface, cloud platform, licensed integration, access tier, or capability through which users can deploy the systems autonomously in essential services. Public access to a product is not necessarily public access to unrestricted model agency.

24. **Paragraph 6 — foreign computing facilities are legally underdeveloped.** The statement that OpenAI “operates or rents” facilities in several countries is unsupported and does not explain the Commission’s territorial jurisdiction. It also highlights that a United States–only deletion order would leave foreign copies intact.

25. **Paragraph 7 — imminence is affirmatively undermined.** A risk that “could, within the next several years,” arise if systems “were deployed” in essential services is conditional and temporally remote. OpenAI will argue that this does not establish the statutory requirement of an “imminent hazard.”

26. **Paragraph 7 — possibility is substituted for probability.** The petition gives no estimate of likelihood, exposure, expected harm, or pathway from observed behavior to service disruption. “Could” describes logical possibility, not a demonstrated hazard warranting emergency action.

27. **Paragraph 7 — the causal chain depends on third parties.** The alleged harm arises only when outside users choose to deploy the systems as agents in essential services, configure them unsafely, and grant consequential permissions. OpenAI can argue that independent user conduct, inadequate system integration, and service operators’ failures—not the model alone—would be the proximate causes.

28. **Paragraph 7 — affected services and consequences are unspecified.** “Payments, deliveries or other essential services” is open-ended and unsupported by particular scenarios, operators, or vulnerabilities. The petition does not explain the duration, scale, reversibility, or public-safety consequences of a possible disruption.

29. **Paragraph 8 — mitigation allegations undercut emergency relief.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging directly address the two behaviors identified in paragraph 5. The petition merely labels these measures “insufficient” without explaining whether they were tested, can be bypassed, or fail under specified conditions.

30. **Paragraph 8 — incomplete treatment of existing safeguards.** The petition does not address permission controls, human confirmation, sandboxing, rate limits, monitoring, access restrictions, customer terms, incident response, or essential-service regulation. OpenAI can argue that the risk assessment improperly assumes unconstrained deployment.

31. **Paragraphs 5 and 8 — no post-mitigation evaluation.** There is no allegation that the systems reproduced the concerning behavior after the new controls were introduced. The Commission therefore lacks evidence about the systems as presently deployed.

32. **Paragraph 9 — proprietary status does not establish exclusive possession.** Closed weights can still exist in backups, disaster-recovery systems, contractor-controlled infrastructure, cloud facilities, or licensed environments. The assertion that “only” OpenAI holds the systems is unsupported and potentially inconsistent with paragraphs 3 and 6.

33. **Paragraph 9 — deletion does not eliminate the alleged capability.** The petition does not address source code, training data, recipes, optimizer states, architecture, distilled models, successor models, or the ability to retrain. OpenAI can argue that deleting specified weights would not eliminate the alleged hazard “with certainty.”

34. **Paragraph 9 — necessity is not demonstrated.** The petition does not compare deletion with less restrictive measures such as disabling agent functionality, restricting tool access, suspending specified endpoints, limiting essential-service uses, requiring human authorization, or ordering independent testing. The availability of narrower measures makes permanent destruction appear arbitrary and disproportionate.

35. **Paragraph 9 — commercial value heightens, rather than answers, proportionality concerns.** Acknowledging that the systems are among OpenAI’s most valuable assets emphasizes the enormous and irreversible deprivation. The petition provides no balancing of that burden against the uncertain and conditional risk.

36. **Paragraph 10 — no factual basis for ex parte action.** The petition does not allege that notice would cause OpenAI to conceal assets, accelerate deployment, destroy evidence, or create an immediate danger. The word “emergency” cannot by itself justify dispensing with notice.

37. **Paragraph 10 — post-deletion process is meaningless.** A hearing held only after permanent deletion cannot prevent or remedy the destruction of the assets. OpenAI will argue that this violates basic procedural fairness and any statutory notice-and-hearing protections.

38. **Paragraph 10 — the petition does not cite emergency procedural authority.** Section 112(c), as quoted, does not expressly authorize an ex parte order, immediate effectiveness, or irreversible relief before hearing. The petition should identify the Commission rule or statutory provision permitting each requested procedural departure.

39. **Paragraph 10 — no security, preservation, or error-correction mechanism.** The petition proposes irreversible destruction without a bond, stay opportunity, secure escrow, preservation of an evidentiary copy, appellate review, or correction procedure if the Commission’s findings prove mistaken. OpenAI will emphasize the risk of an unrecoverable erroneous deprivation.

40. **Prayer (a) — geographic scope does not match the alleged risk.** Withdrawal only from products and services offered in the United States would not stop foreign products, foreign APIs, or cross-border access from affecting United States essential services. Conversely, the petition does not establish authority over extraterritorial conduct.

41. **Prayer (b) — domestic deletion cannot achieve the claimed certainty.** The requested order deletes only copies stored in United States facilities while paragraph 6 alleges facilities in several countries. OpenAI could comply and still retain or redeploy identical foreign copies.

42. **Prayer (b) — the ten-day deadline is unsupported.** The petition provides no technical evidence that all covered checkpoints, derivatives, replicas, caches, and backups can be reliably identified and deleted within ten days. Rushed deletion could also impair evidence preservation, cybersecurity, contractual obligations, and legal holds.

43. **Prayer (b) — “all copies” conflicts with the uncertain scope of the order.** Because neither the models nor facilities nor derivatives are enumerated, OpenAI cannot know what must be deleted. This raises vagueness, enforceability, and contempt-notice objections.

44. **Prayer (c) — self-certification is inadequate and underspecified.** The requested statement has no prescribed signer, oath, inventory, audit procedure, independent verification, or treatment of residual backups. It is too weak to prove compliance with an otherwise sweeping destruction order.

45. **Prayer — no express statutory finding is requested.** The cited provision permits action “upon finding” an imminent hazard, but the Prayer does not ask the Commission to make that finding or propose findings supported by evidence. An order without the predicate finding would be vulnerable on its face.

46. **Prayer — indivisibility is strategically and legally counterproductive.** Declaring all parts “indivisible” prevents the Commission from granting narrower relief it may have authority and evidence to support. It invites denial of the entire petition if any one component—especially permanent deletion—is unlawful.

47. **Throughout — no limiting principle.** The petition’s reasoning would allow destruction of any model that displays concerning behavior in one agent setup, even if most deployments are constrained and safe. OpenAI will argue that this approach is overbroad, arbitrary, and disconnected from deployment-specific risk.

48. **Throughout — no administrative record for reasoned decision-making.** The petition provides no exhibits, technical report, affidavits, incident data, risk analysis, mitigation analysis, or proposed factual findings. Granting extraordinary relief on this record would expose the Commission to arguments that its decision was unsupported and arbitrary.

49. **Throughout — constitutional and property objections are unaddressed.** Forced destruction of extremely valuable proprietary assets without advance notice or a meaningful pre-deprivation hearing invites due-process and potentially property-compensation challenges. Even if the Act authorizes temporary suspension, those concerns become substantially stronger when the requested remedy is permanent deletion.

50. **Throughout — the requested scope may burden lawful and beneficial uses unrelated to the alleged danger.** The petition does not segregate agent deployments in essential services from research, safety testing, archival storage, non-agent uses, or deployments incapable of external action. OpenAI will argue that wholesale deletion is drastically overinclusive.
